A Letter to Our Partners

"Rule No. 1: Never lose money. Rule No. 2: Never forget Rule No. 1." — Warren Buffett

Dear Partners, we are writing to you at a moment that demands absolute clarity. Not optimism. Not pessimism. Clarity. The global financial system, as we enter April 2026, contains more interconnected pressure points than at any time since 2007. We say this not to alarm you, but because you entrust us with your capital and your trust — and both deserve the unvarnished truth.

Charlie Munger taught us that the first step to living wisely is to learn all the ways you can die. In capital markets, the equivalent is mapping every way capital can be permanently impaired before you deploy a single dollar. This report is that map.

Over the following pages, we present the most comprehensive systemic risk analysis our Investment Committee has ever produced. We have identified seven interconnected pressure vectors currently operating across global capital markets. None of them alone is likely to cause a 2008-style collapse. But the connections between them — private credit feeding into commercial real estate, feeding into bank balance sheets, feeding into Treasury market liquidity, feeding into the basis trade, feeding into the very plumbing of the financial system — create a fragility that deserves your full attention.

Here is the most important thing we want you to understand: Fund A was architected precisely for this environment. Every Iron Rule, every constitutional constraint, every deliberate structural choice we have made was designed for the moment when the tide goes out — and, as Buffett famously observed, we discover who has been swimming naked.

We are not swimming naked. We are standing on the shore, fully clothed, with dry powder.

With aloha and unwavering vigilance,
Manish Sainani · Founder, CEO & Investment Committee Chair · Hushh Alpha Aloha Fund A, LP

cards.title: The State of Play: A System Under Stress
cards.html:
Section I

"You only find out who is swimming naked when the tide goes out." — Warren Buffett, 2001 Annual Letter

The global financial system enters April 2026 in a condition best described as structurally fragile but superficially calm. Headline indices remain elevated. Corporate earnings, particularly among the largest technology companies, continue to grow. Unemployment in the United States has stabilized at historically low levels. On the surface, the economy appears resilient.

Beneath the surface, the architecture is cracking. The cracks share a common origin: a decade of ultra-low interest rates created incentives for every participant in the financial system to reach for yield, extend duration, increase leverage, and accept illiquidity in exchange for higher returns. The Federal Reserve's rate-hiking cycle — from near-zero to 5.50%, now eased only modestly to the 3.50–3.75% range — has not yet fully repriced the trillions of dollars in assets originated, structured, and sold during the zero-rate era.

The repricing is happening now. It is happening across seven interconnected vectors simultaneously. The connections between these vectors — the plumbing, the warehouse lines, the cross-collateralization, the repo chains — create transmission mechanisms that could amplify any individual stress event into something far broader.

cards.title: The Liquidity Illusion Shatters
cards.html:
Vector A · Private Credit

"In banking, if everyone wants their money at the same time, there isn't enough money." — Every banking textbook ever written

The private credit market — now approximately $2–3 trillion globally — grew fivefold since the 2008 financial crisis as post-GFC regulation pushed banks out of middle-market lending. For a decade, private credit managers filled that gap and delivered attractive returns with remarkably low defaults. The asset class was marketed to retail and wealth investors through "semi-liquid" vehicles: BDCs, interval funds, and tender offer funds that promised periodic liquidity on fundamentally illiquid underlying assets.

The illusion held as long as more money flowed in than flowed out. That dynamic has now reversed.

cards.title: Three Converging Forces Behind the Crisis
cards.html:
Vector A · Private Credit · Root Causes

1. AI Disruption Hitting the Loan Book Directly

An estimated 15–25% of many private credit portfolios are concentrated in software companies. As generative AI commoditizes coding and SaaS functionality, the enterprise value of these borrowers is eroding — making their high-interest debt loads increasingly unsustainable. A record $25 billion of speculative-rated software loans are trading below 80 cents on the dollar as of January 2026. The very technology everyone was financing is now eating the borrowers.

2. The Structural Liquidity Mismatch: Always a Time Bomb

Loan terms in private credit are typically 3–7 years. Investors in semi-liquid funds can seek redemptions quarterly. That gap only becomes visible when many investors seek cash simultaneously. The products were structurally dishonest — institutional-grade illiquidity sold with retail-grade liquidity promises. This was not a surprise. It was a scheduled collision.

3. Credit Quality Deteriorating Beneath the Surface

Payment-in-kind (PIK) toggles — where borrowers pay interest with more debt instead of cash — are rising across direct lending, a classic late-cycle stress indicator. The Department of Justice has publicly warned about "creative" marks and divergent valuation practices. Shadow defaults (maturity extensions, covenant waivers, amend-and-pretend) are masking the true stress level. The marks are fiction. The losses are real.

cards.title: The Maturity Wall Arrives
cards.html:
Vector B · Commercial Real Estate

"The last one was more of a rip-the-Band-Aid-off kind of approach. This one's slower — pulling the Band-Aid off slowly." — Jim Costello, MSCI

The commercial real estate sector faces the largest refinancing challenge in its history. The Mortgage Bankers Association estimates approximately $875 billion in commercial and multifamily mortgage debt — about 17% of roughly $5 trillion outstanding — is scheduled to mature in 2026. Other estimates, which include loans extended from prior years, put the 2025–2026 combined total at well over $1.5 trillion.

The core problem is simple arithmetic. Borrowers who financed properties at 3–4% in the mid-2010s now face refinancing rates averaging 6.24% — an increase that can destroy the economics of a leveraged real estate investment. Simultaneously, property values have softened, meaning new loans cover a smaller share of current value, forcing owners to inject substantial additional equity or face default.

The "extend and pretend" strategy that defined 2024–2025 is reaching its limits. Of the $957 billion in CRE loans maturing in 2025, only 50–55% were actually paid off. The rest were extended — pushing even more volume into 2026–2027. The extended loans now carry higher interest costs, amortizing structures, and tighter covenants. The problem was deferred, not solved. The wall is higher now than it was twelve months ago.

cards.title: The Elephant in Every Room
cards.html:
Vector C · U.S. Sovereign Debt

"The bond market is the new king in the United States." — Heather Long, Chief Economist, Navy Federal Credit Union

The United States government, by its own Treasury Department's consolidated financial statements for fiscal year 2025, is technically insolvent. Total assets: $6.06 trillion. Total liabilities: $47.78 trillion. The off-balance-sheet picture is more alarming: the 75-year unfunded social insurance obligation surged by $10.1 trillion in a single year, reaching $88.4 trillion. Total federal obligations, if all are included, now exceed $136 trillion — roughly five times U.S. GDP.

The Interest Math

Interest payments on the national debt hit $1.21 trillion in FY2025, consuming 17% of total federal spending — more than the entire defense budget. Every 25 basis point increase in rates adds approximately $95 billion in annual interest costs. Deutsche Bank projects the 2026 deficit will reach 6.7% of GDP.

Fiscal Dominance: The Feedback Loop

When the Federal Reserve raises rates to combat inflation, government interest expense rises immediately — unlike the Volcker era, when debt was only 25% of GDP. This creates a perverse loop: tighter monetary policy worsens the fiscal trajectory, which undermines confidence, which may require even tighter policy. Former Fed Chair Yellen has warned this constraint is real and approaching.

cards.title: Why Our T-Bill Reserve Is the Answer
cards.html:
Vector C · Sovereign Debt · Fund A Positioning

The government must refinance approximately one-third of its outstanding debt in the near term. Treasury Secretary Bessent has acknowledged that long-term debt issuance makes limited economic sense at current rates — trapping the government in a short-duration strategy that maximizes exposure to rate volatility. China's Treasury holdings continue to decline. The TLT (iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF) has fallen nearly 45% from its 2020 highs.

Shortest Duration Available

cards.title: $1.5 Trillion of Hidden Leverage
cards.html:
Vector D · Treasury Basis Trade

"This is beyond fundamentals right now. This is about liquidity." — Jack Chambers, Senior Rates Strategist, ANZ

If there is a single risk vector in this report that could transform a "contained" stress event into a full systemic crisis in a matter of days, it is the Treasury basis trade. The trade itself is mechanically simple: hedge funds buy cash Treasury bonds and simultaneously sell Treasury futures, capturing the small price spread between them. Because the spread is tiny, the trade requires enormous leverage — typically 15 to 20 times invested capital — funded through the overnight repo market.

As of early 2026, the basis trade accounts for an estimated $1 to $2 trillion in gross notional exposure, concentrated among a relatively small number of large multi-strategy hedge funds. The Bank of England, the Financial Stability Board, the SEC, and the CFTC have all formally flagged this as a systemic risk. The regulators are watching. The positions remain.

March 2020 Preview

COVID-19 triggered a global dash for cash. Hedge funds holding basis positions faced margin calls. The selling cascaded — bonds were dumped into thin markets. The Federal Reserve was forced to intervene, buying $100 billion in Treasuries per day at peak.

April 2025 Preview

Tariff fears spiked volatility. Basis trade unwinds pushed 10-year yields past 4.5% and 30-year yields above 5% in a brutal three-day rout — the steepest rate rise since 1981. A preview of what a full unwind looks like.

The Nightmare Scenario

An exogenous shock forces rapid unwinds. Dealers cannot absorb selling. Treasury market liquidity evaporates. Yields spike. The Fed must choose: monetize the debt or allow yields to destroy every leveraged borrower in the system.

Vector D · Critical Interconnection

The Treasury basis trade is not merely a hedge fund risk. It is the keystone risk in the entire global financial system. Understanding this fact is perhaps the most important single insight in this report.

Why the Treasury Market Is Different

The pricing of every financial asset on earth — mortgages, corporate bonds, derivatives, equities, currencies, real estate — is ultimately referenced to Treasury yields. The Treasury market is the risk-free rate from which all other rates derive. A disorderly repricing of the "risk-free" rate is the textbook definition of a systemic event. It is not a sector problem. It is a universal problem.

Fund A's Defense: Structural Impossibility

Our constitutional 1.50x leverage ceiling means we operate at a leverage ratio 10 to 13 times lower than the typical basis trade. We hold no leveraged Treasury positions. We have no repo financing that can be pulled. When basis trade unwinds create forced Treasury selling, we are observers, not participants. We do not receive margin calls. We issue them, metaphorically, by deploying our T-Bill reserve into the dislocated market.

The New York Fed's Standing Repo Facility and expanded central clearing requirements (stretching into 2026) provide some structural defense. But as April 2025 demonstrated, these backstops reduce probability without eliminating risk.

cards.title: The Unregulated Web: NBFI Risk
cards.html:
Vector G · Shadow Banking

The International Monetary Fund's Global Financial Stability Report identifies nonbank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) as one of the primary amplifiers of systemic risk in the current environment. NBFIs operate without deposit insurance protections, mandated liquidity buffers, or direct Federal Reserve supervision. They include private credit funds, hedge funds, BDCs, interval funds, insurance companies with alternative investment portfolios, and the entire chain of repo financing that supports Treasury basis trades.

The IMF's key insight: "The vulnerabilities reinforce each other. An abrupt decline in asset prices or sharp rise in yields could strain banks' balance sheets and pressure open-ended funds. Greater interconnectedness between banks and NBFIs would intensify the transmission of shocks across the financial system."

The traditional Federal Reserve tools have limited direct reach into this sector. Discount window access is unavailable to non-bank lenders. In a stress scenario, the Fed may need to create new emergency lending facilities — similar to those deployed during the 2008 crisis — but the political and institutional challenges of doing so would delay the response and amplify the damage. Delay is what transforms a crisis into a catastrophe.

Fund A's Structural Answer: We operate entirely in regulated public markets with full transparency. We are not part of the NBFI ecosystem. We do not benefit from regulatory arbitrage. We do not have exposure to repo chains, gated funds, or warehouse lines. Our universe is fully liquid, fully transparent, and fully regulated — by design.

Mark Twain is often credited with observing that history doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes. The current environment rhymes with six distinct prior episodes — each of which offers lessons that are directly applicable to the risks we have mapped. Leveraged basis trades in Treasuries; concentrated in a few funds. Lesson: Leverage in "safe" assets can destroy market plumbing overnight.

2000–2002 · Dot-Com

Massive capex on unproven technology; extreme equity overvaluation. Lesson: Even transformative technology can be overpriced; capex + debt = danger.

2006–2008 · GFC

Shadow banking, opaque securitization, liquidity mismatch. Lesson: When you can't find the risk, the risk finds you.

Overnight funding markets seize; Fed forced to intervene. Lesson: Modern finance depends on plumbing no one watches until it breaks.

2020 · COVID Dash

Basis trade unwinds; Treasury illiquidity; emergency QE at $100B/day. Lesson: The Fed can act fast, but the damage in the interregnum is real.

2022 · UK LDI Crisis

Leveraged gilt strategies force pension fund fire sales. Lesson: Leverage in "boring" assets can move sovereign bond markets violently.

The current environment is unique in that it combines elements of all six historical episodes simultaneously. It is a mechanical description of how our constitutional architecture responds to exactly the scenario that destroys others. Covered Call Premiums Increase Volatility drives option premiums higher. The DNSA Engine's overbought call-selling triggers activate when IV rank exceeds the 70th percentile. In a volatile, declining market, we collect more premium per share than in a calm, rising market. We are constitutionally required to be buyers when others are forced sellers. The structure mandates courage when the market demands panic. Share Count Accelerates Upward DRIP-ON (100% premium reinvestment) purchases more shares at lower prices. Automatic repurchase on assignment ensures any shares called away are immediately replaced. The one-way ratchet does not pause in a downturn — it accelerates. Lower prices mean more shares per dollar of premium. cards.html:
Section VII · Actionable Intelligence

Here is what the Investment Committee is actively executing in response to the risk environment documented in this report. We do not believe in research for its own sake. Every insight must connect to a decision. Every risk mapped must correspond to a structural or tactical response. The following five actions represent our current posture.

Maintaining Full Constitutional T-Bill Reserve

The 22% reserve is fully funded and invested in the shortest-duration instruments available. We will not deploy this reserve opportunistically unless our oversold entry signals (RSI <30 weekly, VIX >30, put-call ratio >1.2, widening credit spreads) all fire simultaneously. When they do, we will deploy with size and conviction. The trigger requires all four signals — not just panic, but structural dislocation across multiple dimensions.

Increasing Covered Call Activity at Elevated IV Ranks

With the VIX elevated and implied volatility in the upper quartile for many Alpha Bets 27 positions, we are systematically selling calls at higher strikes and collecting enhanced premiums. Every dollar of premium is immediately reinvested into more shares through DRIP-ON. The current volatility environment is generating premium income at rates well above our long-run assumptions.

Monitoring Bank Interconnection Points in Real Time

We are actively tracking: warehouse lending commitments from major banks to private credit funds; CRE loan delinquency trends by vintage and sector; and CFTC short positioning data for leveraged funds as a proxy for basis trade exposure. Any material deterioration in these metrics will trigger a reduction in our bank and financial services exposure before the market fully prices it in.

Stress-Testing the Alpha Bets 27 Against Each Risk Vector

Every position in the portfolio has been individually assessed for exposure to each of the seven risk vectors. Positions with material software lending exposure (through financial services subsidiaries), excessive AI capex relative to current revenue, or balance-sheet vulnerability to rate spikes have been flagged for potential position-size reduction at the next rebalancing.

Preparing for Opportunistic Deployment: The Berkshire Playbook

If the contagion map progresses to stages 3–5, some of the world's best businesses will trade at prices not seen since 2022 or earlier. Our T-Bill Reserve, combined with the cash-secured put framework, positions us to acquire shares in Aces and Kings at historically attractive valuations. This is the Berkshire playbook: be greedy when others are fearful — but only if you have the capital and the constitutional discipline to act. We have both.

cards.title: The King of All Strategies: Absolute Free Cash Flow Growth
cards.html:
Our Investment Philosophy

Before we conclude, we want to state our core investment philosophy with the clarity it deserves. This is not just a risk management report. It is a declaration of what we believe with the conviction of mathematicians, physicists, and engineers who have studied capital markets with the same rigor applied to the hardest problems in science.

Finding the fastest absolute free cash flow growing businesses in the fastest growing markets and industries — businesses that are globally profitable and compounding — is the King of the King of the King of all investment strategies.

Free cash flow is the oxygen of enterprise. Everything else — earnings, revenue, EBITDA, operating income — is accounting. Free cash flow is reality. It is what a business can actually do: pay dividends, buy back shares, reinvest in growth, acquire competitors, or simply hold as ammunition. When free cash flow grows at 20%, 30%, or 40% per year — compounding, relentlessly, in the fastest growing industries of the global economy — the math becomes extraordinary over a five to ten year horizon.

We only pick the elite Aces of Aces of Aces. The top 27 businesses in the world by this single criterion. And we hold them with the discipline of a physicist who knows that a well-designed system, left to operate without interference, produces extraordinary results.

cards.title: What Makes an Ace of Aces?
cards.html:
The Alpha Bets Framework

The Alpha Bets 27 portfolio is not built on narrative or momentum or analyst consensus. It is built on a single, rigorous, mathematically precise question: Which businesses are growing their absolute free cash flow fastest, in the fastest growing global markets, with the highest probability of sustaining that growth for the next decade? The answer to that question, applied with institutional rigor, produces a portfolio that is fundamentally different from any index or peer fund.

Absolute FCF Growth Rate

We measure free cash flow growth in absolute dollar terms, not just percentage growth. A business growing FCF from $50B to $75B ($25B added) is more valuable than one growing from $1B to $1.5B (same percentage, different scale). Absolute growth wins markets and compounds LP wealth.

Fastest Growing Global Markets

We require that our Aces compete in markets with structural tailwinds: AI infrastructure, digital advertising, cloud computing, semiconductor ecosystems, global e-commerce, financial technology. Markets that are not merely growing, but accelerating.

Durable Competitive Moat

FCF machines that cannot be easily disrupted. Network effects, switching costs, regulatory barriers, proprietary data advantages, and platform economics that make the dominant business more dominant with each passing year — the flywheel that never stops spinning.

Globally Profitable, Not Just U.S.-Centric

Our Aces generate free cash flow across multiple continents and currencies. Geographic diversification of revenue provides natural hedging against any single economy's downturn while giving the business access to the fastest-growing consumer and enterprise markets worldwide.

"The best model of a chicken is a chicken." — attributed to the philosophy of model-building that Jim Simons embodied — reality first, always.

Simons' legacy teaches us that the edge in investing is not information. It is the discipline to use information correctly, without the cognitive biases, the fear, the greed, and the narrative fallacies that cause even the most brilliant human minds to make predictable errors at predictable times. The Medallion Fund's 66% gross annual return over three decades was not luck. It was mathematics applied with absolute consistency.

cards.title: Fortune Favors the Prepared
cards.html:
Section VIII · Conclusion

"The best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago. The second best time is now." — Chinese Proverb

We began this report with a promise of clarity. Let us end with it. The global financial system is fragile. Seven interconnected risk vectors create a surface area for disruption larger than at any time since 2007. The private credit liquidity crisis is not a future risk — it is happening today. The commercial real estate maturity wall is not a hypothetical — it is a mathematical certainty that $875 billion in loans must be refinanced this year. The Treasury basis trade is not a theoretical danger — it is $1.5 trillion in notional exposure running at 20x leverage. The AI capex cycle is being financed by the same private credit system that is simultaneously gating redemptions.

None of this means a crisis is inevitable. Markets have a remarkable capacity to absorb stress, extend timelines, and muddle through. The Federal Reserve has more tools than it had in 2008. Banks are better capitalized than before the GFC. And the underlying businesses that anchor the global economy — many of which sit in our Alpha Bets 27 portfolio — generate unprecedented levels of free cash flow.

But hope is not a strategy. And the history of finance is unambiguous: the catastrophes that destroy generational wealth are never the ones everyone is watching. They are the ones hiding in the connections between risks that look manageable in isolation.
